title: On the trade-off between expressivity and privacy in graph representation learning
claim: Privacy noise blurs embeddings of near-identical inputs into overlap while distant inputs stay separable, exposing a tension between distinguishability and privacy.
layout: 3 graphs on top, 1-D axis with Gaussian bumps below, left-to-right
description: The figure has two rows. The top row shows three small black node-and-edge graphs labeled G1, G2 and G3, spaced horizontally. G1 is a house shape: a square with a triangle roof. G2 is a diamond with a tail. G3 is a star with four leaves. A horizontal arrow axis runs along the bottom. Black squares on it mark the embeddings φ(G1), φ(G2) and φ(G3), each under its graph. Above each square sits a filled Gaussian bump with a dotted vertical line at its center. G1's bump is orange and G2's is lavender. They sit close together and overlap heavily, with a darker overlap region. G3's bump is green and sits far to the right, clearly separate. The eye goes first to the overlapping orange and lavender bumps. These show that the privacy noise makes the two similar graphs hard to tell apart.
caption: G1 and G2 are two non-isomorphic graphs that differ in exactly one edge. An expressive graph algorithm should distinguish between these graphs and provide different embeddings φ(G1)̸ = φ(G2); a differentially private algorithm instead ensures that φ(G1) ≈φ(G2).
abstract: We investigate the trade-off between expressive power and privacy guarantees in graph representation learning. Privacy-preserving machine learning faces growing regulatory demands that pose a fundamental challenge: safeguarding sensitive data while maintaining expressive power. To address this challenge, we leverage homomorphism density vectors to obtain graph embeddings that are private and expressive. Homomorphism densities are provably highly discriminative and offer a powerful tool for distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs. By adding noise calibrated to each density’s sensitivity, we ensure that the resulting embeddings satisfy formal differential privacy guarantees. Our theoretical construction preserves expressivity in expectation, as each private embedding remains unbiased with respect to the true homomorphism densities. We demonstrate the usefulness of our embeddings through experiments on molecular and social network datasets.
